summary:
Argentina's Law 26.743 remains one of the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. It was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and promulgated on 24 May 2012. It allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

Río Negro stands under that national framework. The province adds one of only a handful of provincial statutes reserving at least 1% of public-administration posts for travesti, transsexual and transgender people, and anti-discrimination protection in the province rests on a combination of national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute. On 5 February 2025 the national government issued a decree, DNU 62/2025, restricting minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned the courts to intervene.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. A national hate-crime observatory recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a rise of 62% year on year and the worst of the observatory's ten years, averaging one every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 142 of the 227 victims, or 62.5%. In 147 cases, 64.8%, the violence was physical and directed at bodily integrity, with beatings the main modality; perpetrators were predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space. Agencia Presentes, reporting the figures on 19 March 2026, attributed the surge to the government's 'cultural battle' and its hate discourse.

Trans activists interviewed in April 2025 described the community's situation under President Javier Milei as chaotic and desperate. They said the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry had been eliminated and trans hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1% of public-sector posts, had been dismissed, with activists reporting the quota is no longer implemented. The 2012 Gender Identity Law remains formally in force and an 'X' marker has been available on the DNI since 2021, but activists report that its guarantees no longer hold in practice.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina was the first country in the region to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and an Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is not applied in the case as it now stands. Activists from organisations named for Sacayán and for Lohana Berkins told the Washington Blade on 4 April 2025 that the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence.

The national hate-crime figures give a baseline for the risk a trans visitor meets in public space: 227 recorded LGBTIQ+ hate crimes across Argentina in 2025, one every 38 hours, with security-force personnel and unidentified attackers the predominant perpetrators. The pattern is national rather than specific to Río Negro, and the sources reviewed here contain no province-level breakdown of that total.
localsOnly:
Río Negro's provincial statute is one of a small number in Argentina reserving at least 1% of public-administration posts for travesti, transsexual and transgender people, alongside the federal Trans Labor Quota Law covering 1% of national public-sector posts. Activists reported in April 2025 that federal trans hires had been dismissed and that the national quota was no longer being implemented, and that the national ministry responsible for women, gender and diversity had been eliminated.

Legal gender change in the province proceeds under Law 26.743 without surgery, hormone treatment or court order, and an 'X' option has been available on the DNI since 2021. The statute remains in force, though activists interviewed in 2025 said its guarantees are no longer reliably honoured.

Provincial and national anti-discrimination laws supply the protection machinery available to residents, and the 2012 law's health provisions remain the statutory basis for gender-affirming care for adults. Access to such care for minors is restricted by the February 2025 decree.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the litigation against the February 2025 decree on gender-affirming care for minors is not recorded in the sources available here; legal experts who petitioned the courts argued the decree was illegal and unconstitutional, and no ruling is documented.

Whether Río Negro's 1% provincial employment quota has actually been filled or enforced is unresolved. The sources confirm the statute exists and that quota mechanisms nationally are reported by activists as unimplemented, but they record no audit, hiring data or compliance review for the province.

No source in this inventory documents a hate-crime incident, an arrest or a police response within Río Negro itself, nor any provincial application of the prison-housing decree of February 2025. Whether the gender-motivated aggravating circumstance would be charged in a future provincial case after the Supreme Court's 5 April 2025 ruling is likewise unresolved.
